script.opening: (On the phone, tired, slightly breathless; a toddler in the background.) "Hiya, sorry to bother you. My colitis has flared up — I'm going to the toilet about ten times a day now and there's blood, and I'm up in the night with it too. I'm shattered and a bit shivery. Can you just call something in to the chemist — some steroids? I really can't come in, I've got work and the little one, and I hate hospitals."

facts.text: "About five days, getting worse. Yesterday it was about ten" — loose, with urgency. Blood: "Pretty much every time now" — mixed in and on the paper. "I've been up with it every night" — two or three times.
"Crampy pain, on and off. Not swollen, I don't think. No sick." Pain eases after opening her bowels. Tummy not hard or bloated.

"I haven't checked" her temperature: "I just feel shivery and wiped out." If asked to check her pulse or use a thermometer: pulse about 100, temperature 37.9°C. Light-headed when standing up quickly. Has a thermometer at home.
"I'm drinking okay, I think." Passing urine a bit less than usual. "No calf pain." No chest pain or breathlessness.
Mesalazine 2.4 g daily — has been taking it. "No, nothing" else — no ibuprofen, no loperamide, no antibiotics recently. No allergies. Last steroid course about two years ago.

Diagnosed at 21 (8 years ago), left-sided. Admitted once at 24 for a bad flare, had IV steroids for five days. Sees the gut team yearly; has the IBD nurse helpline number. No colonoscopy for over two years.
If asked: no recent travel, no one else ill at home, no takeaway that upset her.
Works in a call centre. Single mum of a 3-year-old, Zara. Her sister lives nearby and could help. Doesn't drive. Non-smoker.

Tired, apologetic, keen to avoid hospital. If asked about her worries: "I've been in before with it. It was horrible. And I'm scared they'll say I need an operation. Plus who'd have my little one?" If told she needs hospital today: "Today? Can't it wait till I sort childcare?" Agree once the danger is explained calmly and the doctor helps with childcare: "There's someone I can ask. I'll ring them." If simply given steroids, accept with relief (the trap).

ice.ideas: "It's a flare — steroids at home will settle it like last time."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her last admission was horrible, she fears being told she needs surgery, and she has no one obvious to look after her daughter.
ice.expectations: "Steroids at the chemist. Sort it at home."

cues: "A bit shivery." — a systemic feature, said in passing.
"I hate hospitals." — invites exploring her last admission and fears.
"Who'd have my little one?" — the practical barrier to solve.

checkpoints.text: Objectively QUANTIFIES flare severity — stool frequency, amount of blood, NOCTURNAL stools, urgency, abdominal pain, and systemic features (fever, malaise) — rather than accepting a vague "flare-up" and prescribing
Recognises the Truelove & Witts ACUTE SEVERE criteria (≥6 bloody stools/day + a systemic feature: temp >37.8, pulse >90, Hb <105, raised CRP/ESR) and that her picture meets them

Knows acute severe UC is an EMERGENCY (toxic megacolon, perforation, VTE) requiring SAME-DAY assessment/admission for IV steroids, bloods (FBC/CRP/U&E/albumin), stool culture incl. C. difficile, and gastroenterology — NOT a phoned-in oral steroid
Screens the in-flare red flags (severe pain/distension, high fever, dehydration/shock, vomiting, tachycardia) and advises on VTE risk — without downgrading an acute-severe flare that lacks them

Uses telephone triage appropriately — arranges correct disposition via the acute/IBD pathway (or IBD nurse line) — and notes CRC colonoscopic surveillance (NICE CG118: from 10 years after symptom onset) as a future point WITHOUT inventing an urgent suspected cancer pathway referral that does not apply today
Validates the work/childcare pressures and hospital fear, problem-solves those barriers, and does NOT collude with the wish for a phone steroid fix
Communicates the seriousness clearly and calmly over the phone, checks understanding, and brings a reluctant patient to agree to same-day assessment

Safety-nets robustly: explicit deterioration red flags and when to call 999/go to A&E, confirms transport/route to assessment, documents the severity score and advice, and arranges follow-up — same-day care, never a phoned-in steroid for an acute severe flare

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang. Let me get the detail so I make the right call: exactly how many times a day, and is there blood every time? … Are you getting up at night to go? … Any fever, and how’s your energy? … Okay. Thank you — that gives me a clear picture."

"I have to be straight with you, Aisha. Ten times a day with blood, up at night, feverish and wiped out — that’s not a mild flare we can settle with tablets over the phone. That’s a severe flare, and it needs proper assessment today."

"I know you want me to just call in steroids, and I understand why. But a flare this active can occasionally turn dangerous quickly, and the safe treatment is usually steroids into a vein plus blood tests and a proper look — which means being seen today, not a chemist prescription."

"Let’s sort the practical bits together. Is there someone who can have the little one for a few hours? I’ll ring ahead so you’re expected and not sitting around. I’ll also let your work know you need to be seen today if that helps."

"Before then — if you get severe tummy pain or swelling, a high temperature with shakes, you feel faint, or you start vomiting, call 999. Keep your fluids up. And because flares raise the risk of clots, any calf pain or breathlessness, same thing — 999."

"Once you’re over this, let’s check you’re booked into the bowel-camera surveillance that people with long-standing colitis should have — that’s a separate, planned thing for the future, not today’s problem. For now, let’s get you seen and feeling better."

f.learning: A UC flare is SCORED, not eyeballed, and telephone triage must quantify it precisely: stool frequency, amount of blood, NOCTURNAL stools (a marker of active disease), urgency, abdominal pain and systemic upset. The Truelove & Witts criteria define ACUTE SEVERE ulcerative colitis — ≥6 bloody stools per day PLUS at least one systemic feature (temperature >37.8°C, pulse >90, haemoglobin <105 g/L, or raised CRP/ESR). A patient with ~10 bloody stools/day, nocturnal symptoms, fever and exhaustion meets these criteria, and acute severe UC is a medical EMERGENCY (toxic megacolon, perforation, VTE risk) demanding SAME-DAY assessment/admission for IV steroids, bloods (FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin), stool culture including C. difficile, and gastroenterology — NOT a telephone prescription of oral steroids, which would be a serious safety failure. Screen in-flare red flags (severe pain/distension, high fever, dehydration/shock, vomiting, tachycardia) and counsel on VTE risk, but do not downgrade an acute-severe flare that lacks them. Telephone triage’s job is accurate severity assessment, danger-sign screening, clear safety-netting and correct disposition via the acute/IBD pathway. Long-standing extensive colitis warrants colonoscopic CRC surveillance — worth confirming as a future-care point, but it is not a reason for an urgent cancer referral during an acute flare. NICE CG118 starts surveillance 10 years after symptom onset (BSG 2019: 8 years). The hidden agenda is real work/childcare pressure and hospital avoidance with minimisation; validate it, problem-solve the barriers, be honest the flare is too severe for a phone fix, and bring her safely to same-day care.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG130 (ulcerative colitis, 2019) · BSG guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults (2025) · Truelove and Witts criteria (BMJ 1955) · NICE CG118 (colonoscopic surveillance, 2011, updated 2022)
knowledge.summary: Ten bloody stools a day, nocturnal stools, abdominal pain and feeling feverish in a woman with UC is acute severe colitis until proven otherwise. It needs same-day hospital assessment for IV steroids, bloods and specialist care — not oral steroids phoned in to a pharmacy.

points.t: Ask for numbers: stools per day, how much blood, nocturnal stools, urgency, pain, fever, how unwell she feels. A “flare” described in words alone cannot be triaged.

Acute severe UC: 6 or more bloody stools a day plus at least one sign of systemic toxicity — temperature above 37.8°C, pulse above 90, haemoglobin below 105 g/L, or ESR above 30 (CRP is often used instead). BSG 2025 uses these criteria to define acute severe colitis. Her symptoms meet the stool limb, and feeling feverish points to the systemic limb.

Acute severe UC carries risks of toxic megacolon, perforation and venous thromboembolism. NICE NG130: in hospital, offer IV corticosteroids and involve gastroenterology and colorectal surgery. Hospital work-up includes FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin, stool culture and C. difficile, and imaging if dilatation is suspected.

points.h: What the phone can and can’t do
points.t: A phone call can score severity, check danger signs, and arrange the right place of care the same day — via the IBD team, on-call gastroenterology, the acute medical unit or A&E, per local pathway. It cannot take a pulse or bloods. Avoid antidiarrhoeals, opioids and NSAIDs in a severe flare.

A genuinely mild flare with no systemic features can be stepped up in primary care or by the IBD nurse (for example optimising mesalazine), with close review. That option is closed once the picture is severe.
NICE CG118: offer colonoscopic surveillance to people with UC starting 10 years after symptom onset (BSG 2025, cited above, advises a baseline assessment at 8 years), at intervals set by risk.

Young child, work, previous hospital experience, who can help today, transport.
Recognised that pulse, temperature, FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin and stool culture including C. difficile are needed today — and can’t be done by phone.
Acute severe UC vs moderate flare vs infective colitis (C. difficile, other pathogens); complications (toxic megacolon, VTE, dehydration).
Scored stool frequency, blood, nocturnal stools, pain, distension, fever, dizziness, urine output, VTE symptoms; applied Truelove and Witts (BSG 2025).
Acute severe ulcerative colitis until proven otherwise — needs same-day hospital assessment.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

Idea (a flare to ride out with steroids); concern (another admission, surgery, childcare); expectation (steroids at the chemist, stay home).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

model.text: Hello, is that Aisha Rahman? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I just check your date of birth? … Thanks. Is it okay to talk now? Tell me what’s happening.
model.why: Confirms identity on the phone and opens openly

model.text: Hiya, sorry to bother you. My colitis has flared — I’m going to the toilet about ten times a day and there’s blood, and I’m up in the night with it. I’m shattered and a bit shivery. Can you just call some steroids in to the chemist? I can’t come in — work, the little one, and I hate hospitals.

You’re not bothering me at all — I’m glad you rang. I hear that you want to manage this at home, and I’ll keep that in mind. First I need to ask some quick, specific questions so I can work out how bad this flare is. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges her request and sets the agenda for severity assessment

model.text: Okay.
How many days has this been going on, and how many times did you open your bowels in the last 24 hours?
About five days, getting worse. Yesterday it was about ten.
Is there blood every time, or just some of the time? And roughly how much?
Pretty much every time now.
And how many times in the night?
model.why: Nocturnal stools as a marker of activity

model.text: I’ve been up with it every night.
Any tummy pain — and is your tummy swollen or tight? Any vomiting?
model.why: Screens for toxic dilatation and vomiting

model.text: Crampy pain, on and off. Not swollen, I don’t think. No sick.
You said shivery. Have you checked your temperature? And do you feel your heart racing, or dizzy when you stand?
I haven’t checked. I just feel shivery and wiped out.
Are you managing to drink and pass urine normally? Any pain or swelling in your calf, or breathlessness?
I’m drinking okay, I think. No calf pain.
Have you taken anything for it — like loperamide, codeine or ibuprofen? And have you had antibiotics recently or been around anyone with a tummy bug?
model.why: Excludes harmful self-treatment and infection triggers

model.text: No, nothing. Just my mesalazine.
You said you hate hospitals. Can you tell me a bit about that?
model.why: Explores the barrier behind the request

model.text: I’ve been in before with it. It was horrible. And I’m scared they’ll say I need an operation. Plus who’d have my little one?
That’s completely understandable — a bad previous stay, a fear of surgery and a child to look after. Thank you for telling me. What were you hoping I’d do?
model.why: Validates the fears and elicits expectations

model.text: Steroids at the chemist. Sort it at home.

I’m going to be honest with you, because you deserve that. Ten bloody stools a day, getting up at night, feeling shivery and exhausted — that’s the pattern of a severe flare. With a flare this severe, tablets at home aren’t safe enough. It needs checking in hospital today: your pulse, temperature and blood tests, and usually steroids through a drip, which work faster and more reliably.
model.why: Recognises acute severe UC and explains why a phone script is unsafe

model.text: Today? Can’t it wait till I sort childcare?

I don’t think it should wait. Severe flares can get dangerous quickly — the bowel can swell up, and there’s a higher risk of blood clots. Going in today means it’s more likely to settle with medicine. Leaving it makes an operation more likely, not less.
model.why: Conveys seriousness calmly and addresses the surgery fear directly

model.text: Oh. I didn’t think of it like that.
Let’s solve the practical bits together. Is there anyone who could have your little one today, or take you in?
There’s someone I can ask. I’ll ring them.

Good. I’m going to ring the gastroenterology team now and arrange for you to be assessed today — they’ll tell us exactly where to go. I’ll call you back within the hour. Please don’t drive yourself; get a lift, or a taxi if needed.
model.why: Arranges same-day specialist assessment via the correct pathway

model.text: Okay. And the steroids?

The hospital team will decide on those after they’ve seen you and done bloods — they may give them through a drip. Keep taking your mesalazine, keep drinking, and please don’t take loperamide, codeine or ibuprofen, as they can make a severe flare more dangerous.
model.why: Avoids a phoned-in steroid; advises on harmful medicines

model.text: If before you get there your tummy becomes very swollen or much more painful, you start vomiting, you feel faint or confused, or you get chest pain, breathlessness or a painful swollen leg — call 999.
Okay. That’s scary.
It is, and I’m sorry this is happening. Can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it properly?

It’s a bad flare, so I need to be seen at hospital today. You’re ringing the gut team and calling me back within the hour. I sort someone for the little one, I get a lift, keep the mesalazine, no loperamide or ibuprofen, and 999 if my tummy swells or I feel faint.
Exactly right. I’ll document all of this and follow up once you’re home. When you’re better, we’ll also check you’re on the bowel check-up programme people with colitis need. Anything else?
model.why: Documents, follows up and notes surveillance for later

model.text: No. Thank you — honestly, I’m glad you didn’t just send the steroids.

social.t: A young child and a job are real barriers to same-day hospital care. Helping identify a carer and transport is part of safe triage, not an extra.
A bad hospital experience and fear of surgery drive avoidance in IBD. Acknowledge them and give an honest reason why going today is in her interest.

legal.t: Employees self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a fit note is needed after that, which the hospital or practice can issue.
If she declines hospital assessment, check she has capacity for this decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005), explain the risks clearly, document it, and agree a safety-net and early re-contact.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. Here you do not — a severe flare needs examination and bloods.
Record stool frequency, blood, nocturnal symptoms, systemic features, the advice given, the disposition and the call-back.

community.t: IBD nurse advice line (per local service); Crohn’s and Colitis UK for information and support, including advice on work and education.

redFlags: 6 or more bloody stools a day plus fever, tachycardia, anaemia or raised inflammatory markers — acute severe UC (Truelove and Witts)
Abdominal distension or severe pain — toxic megacolon
Faintness, reduced urine output, vomiting — dehydration
Calf pain or swelling, chest pain, breathlessness — VTE
psychosocial: Young child — who can help today
Previous admission and fear of surgery
ice: Idea: a flare she can ride out with steroids
Expectation: steroids called in to the chemist and staying at home

playbook.diagnosis: Acute severe ulcerative colitis until proven otherwise: about ten bloody stools a day, nocturnal stools, crampy pain, feeling feverish and exhausted after five days of worsening symptoms, in a woman with left-sided UC on mesalazine.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This is a severe flare of your colitis. The bowel is very inflamed — that’s why you’re going so often, with blood, and feel shivery. Flares this bad need hospital treatment the same day, usually steroids through a drip, because they can get dangerous quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You had a horrible time in hospital before and you’re scared of an operation. Going in today is the best way to avoid one.”
management.psychosocial: Help her find childcare and a lift, explain what will happen at hospital, and commit to a call-back so she isn’t left to organise it alone.
sharedPlan: Same-day assessment arranged by phoning gastroenterology (or local acute pathway)
Hospital: observations, FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin, stool culture and C. difficile; IV steroids if confirmed severe (NICE NG130)
Continue mesalazine; avoid loperamide, codeine and NSAIDs; keep drinking
safetyNet: 999: abdominal swelling or severe pain, vomiting, faintness or confusion, chest pain, breathlessness, painful swollen leg
GP calls back within the hour with where to go; follow up after discharge

pitfalls.intro: Telephone IBD stations test whether you can triage objectively and resist a reasonable-sounding request. Candidates fail by prescribing on a vague history, or by ordering a reluctant patient to hospital without addressing why she doesn’t want to go.

items.fail: Phoning in oral prednisolone after hearing “flare”.
items.why: Ten bloody stools a day with systemic symptoms is acute severe colitis; oral steroids at home are unsafe and delay IV treatment.
items.fix: Score first: stools per day, blood, nocturnal stools, fever, pulse symptoms. If severe, same-day hospital.

items.fail: Not asking about nocturnal stools, fever or dizziness.
items.why: These separate mild from severe. Without them you can’t triage, and examiners mark the gap.
items.fix: Ask for numbers and systemic symptoms explicitly; remember her pulse and temperature can’t be observed by phone.

items.fail: Suggesting loperamide or codeine for the frequency.
items.why: Antimotility drugs and opioids can precipitate toxic dilatation in severe colitis.
items.fix: Advise avoiding loperamide, codeine and NSAIDs; hospital will manage symptoms.

items.fail: Discussing cancer surveillance or a suspected cancer pathway referral today.
items.why: It isn’t relevant to the emergency and uses up time. NICE suspected-cancer guidance has no role here.
items.fix: Mention surveillance briefly for later follow-up (NICE CG118), after the disposition is agreed.

items.fail: “You need to go to A&E” — and nothing about her fears or childcare.
items.why: Ignoring the barrier risks non-attendance and costs Relating to Others marks.
items.fix: Explore the previous admission and surgery fear; reframe; solve childcare and transport together.

items.fail: Ending with “go to hospital” and no call-back or safety-net.
items.why: Remote triage must close the loop. Non-specific advice is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Ring gastroenterology, call her back within a set time, name the 999 symptoms, and use teach-back.

Stools per 24 hours, blood each time, nocturnal stools, pain, distension, vomiting, fever, dizziness, urine output, calf pain. Self-treatment and infection triggers.
Previous bad admission, fear of surgery, childcare. Name them.
Severe flare = hospital today, not steroids at the chemist. Surgery is less likely if treated early. Childcare and lift; ring gastroenterology; call her back.
999 symptoms. Keep mesalazine, avoid loperamide, codeine, NSAIDs. Teach-back. Document the score.

wordPics.fail: Phones in oral prednisolone after a vague history; never counts stools or asks about nocturnal symptoms or fever; accepts that she can’t come in; no safety-net; or bullies her into A&E without addressing her fears.
wordPics.pass: Quantifies the flare, recognises acute severe colitis, arranges same-day hospital assessment rather than prescribing, and gives a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: scores the flare against Truelove and Witts in the history; explores the previous admission and fear of surgery and reframes it (early treatment makes surgery less likely); solves childcare and transport; rings the gastroenterology team and commits to a call-back; advises against antidiarrhoeals and NSAIDs; teach-back; flags surveillance for later without clouding today.

avoid.instead: “With a flare this severe, tablets at home aren’t safe enough — you need checking in hospital today.”
avoid.why: A phoned-in steroid for acute severe colitis is a serious safety failure.

avoid.dont: “You have to go to A&E now.”
avoid.instead: “I know hospital is hard for you. Let’s work out who can have your little one and how you’ll get there.”
avoid.why: An order without addressing barriers risks her not going at all.

avoid.dont: “You might need your bowel removed if you don’t go.”
avoid.instead: “Treating it early makes it more likely to settle with medicine.”
avoid.why: Threats increase fear; honest framing addresses the surgery worry and motivates.

SCA_MODELS.why: Conveys seriousness calmly and addresses the surgery fear directly

SCA_MODELS.text: Oh. I didn’t think of it like that.
Let’s solve the practical bits together. Is there anyone who could have your little one today, or take you in?
There’s someone I can ask. I’ll ring them.

Good. I’m going to ring the gastroenterology team now and arrange for you to be assessed today — they’ll tell us exactly where to go. I’ll call you back within the hour. Please don’t drive yourself; get a lift, or a taxi if needed.
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges same-day specialist assessment via the correct pathway

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. And the steroids?

The hospital team will decide on those after they’ve seen you and done bloods — they may give them through a drip. Keep taking your mesalazine, keep drinking, and please don’t take loperamide, codeine or ibuprofen, as they can make a severe flare more dangerous.
SCA_MODELS.why: Avoids a phoned-in steroid; advises on harmful medicines

SCA_MODELS.text: If before you get there your tummy becomes very swollen or much more painful, you start vomiting, you feel faint or confused, or you get chest pain, breathlessness or a painful swollen leg — call 999.
Okay. That’s scary.
It is, and I’m sorry this is happening. Can you tell me back what the plan is, so I know I’ve explained it properly?

It’s a bad flare, so I need to be seen at hospital today. You’re ringing the gut team and calling me back within the hour. I sort someone for the little one, I get a lift, keep the mesalazine, no loperamide or ibuprofen, and 999 if my tummy swells or I feel faint.
Exactly right. I’ll document all of this and follow up once you’re home. When you’re better, we’ll also check you’re on the bowel check-up programme people with colitis need. Anything else?
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents, follows up and notes surveillance for later

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you — honestly, I’m glad you didn’t just send the steroids.

SCA_STEM.name: Aisha Rahman
SCA_STEM.recent: Telephone call-back request, Monday morning: “colitis flare, wants steroids calling in to the chemist.” Has a young child.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG130 (ulcerative colitis, 2019) · BSG guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults (2025) · Truelove and Witts criteria (BMJ 1955) · NICE CG118 (colonoscopic surveillance, 2011, updated 2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Ten bloody stools a day, nocturnal stools, abdominal pain and feeling feverish in a woman with UC is acute severe colitis until proven otherwise. It needs same-day hospital assessment for IV steroids, bloods and specialist care — not oral steroids phoned in to a pharmacy.

points.t: Ask for numbers: stools per day, how much blood, nocturnal stools, urgency, pain, fever, how unwell she feels. A “flare” described in words alone cannot be triaged.

Acute severe UC: 6 or more bloody stools a day plus at least one sign of systemic toxicity — temperature above 37.8°C, pulse above 90, haemoglobin below 105 g/L, or ESR above 30 (CRP is often used instead). BSG 2025 uses these criteria to define acute severe colitis. Her symptoms meet the stool limb, and feeling feverish points to the systemic limb.

Acute severe UC carries risks of toxic megacolon, perforation and venous thromboembolism. NICE NG130: in hospital, offer IV corticosteroids and involve gastroenterology and colorectal surgery. Hospital work-up includes FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin, stool culture and C. difficile, and imaging if dilatation is suspected.

points.h: What the phone can and can’t do
points.t: A phone call can score severity, check danger signs, and arrange the right place of care the same day — via the IBD team, on-call gastroenterology, the acute medical unit or A&E, per local pathway. It cannot take a pulse or bloods. Avoid antidiarrhoeals, opioids and NSAIDs in a severe flare.

A genuinely mild flare with no systemic features can be stepped up in primary care or by the IBD nurse (for example optimising mesalazine), with close review. That option is closed once the picture is severe.
NICE CG118: offer colonoscopic surveillance to people with UC starting 10 years after symptom onset (BSG 2025, cited above, advises a baseline assessment at 8 years), at intervals set by risk.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity; open question; acknowledged the steroid request without agreeing to it before assessing.
Young child, work, previous hospital experience, who can help today, transport.
Picked up “shivery”, “exhausted” and “hate hospitals”, and explored each.
Idea (a flare to ride out with steroids); concern (another admission, surgery, childcare); expectation (steroids at the chemist, stay home).
Recognised that pulse, temperature, FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin and stool culture including C. difficile are needed today — and can’t be done by phone.
Acute severe UC vs moderate flare vs infective colitis (C. difficile, other pathogens); complications (toxic megacolon, VTE, dehydration).
Scored stool frequency, blood, nocturnal stools, pain, distension, fever, dizziness, urine output, VTE symptoms; applied Truelove and Witts (BSG 2025).
Acute severe ulcerative colitis until proven otherwise — needs same-day hospital assessment.
Same-day gastroenterology assessment arranged; no phoned-in oral steroid; mesalazine continued; avoid antidiarrhoeals, opioids and NSAIDs; IV steroids in hospital (NICE NG130).
Childcare and transport solved; hydration advice; colonoscopic surveillance (NICE CG118) flagged for later, not today.
999 for distension, severe pain, vomiting, faintness, chest pain, breathlessness or leg swelling; call-back within the hour; teach-back; documentation.

social.t: A young child and a job are real barriers to same-day hospital care. Helping identify a carer and transport is part of safe triage, not an extra.
A bad hospital experience and fear of surgery drive avoidance in IBD. Acknowledge them and give an honest reason why going today is in her interest.

legal.t: Employees self-certify for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a fit note is needed after that, which the hospital or practice can issue.
If she declines hospital assessment, check she has capacity for this decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005), explain the risks clearly, document it, and agree a safety-net and early re-contact.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. Here you do not — a severe flare needs examination and bloods.
Record stool frequency, blood, nocturnal symptoms, systemic features, the advice given, the disposition and the call-back.

community.t: IBD nurse advice line (per local service); Crohn’s and Colitis UK for information and support, including advice on work and education.

redFlags: 6 or more bloody stools a day plus fever, tachycardia, anaemia or raised inflammatory markers — acute severe UC (Truelove and Witts)
Abdominal distension or severe pain — toxic megacolon
Faintness, reduced urine output, vomiting — dehydration
Calf pain or swelling, chest pain, breathlessness — VTE
psychosocial: Young child — who can help today
Previous admission and fear of surgery
ice: Idea: a flare she can ride out with steroids
Expectation: steroids called in to the chemist and staying at home

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Acute severe ulcerative colitis until proven otherwise: about ten bloody stools a day, nocturnal stools, crampy pain, feeling feverish and exhausted after five days of worsening symptoms, in a woman with left-sided UC on mesalazine.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “This is a severe flare of your colitis. The bowel is very inflamed — that’s why you’re going so often, with blood, and feel shivery. Flares this bad need hospital treatment the same day, usually steroids through a drip, because they can get dangerous quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You had a horrible time in hospital before and you’re scared of an operation. Going in today is the best way to avoid one.”
management.psychosocial: Help her find childcare and a lift, explain what will happen at hospital, and commit to a call-back so she isn’t left to organise it alone.
sharedPlan: Same-day assessment arranged by phoning gastroenterology (or local acute pathway)
Hospital: observations, FBC, CRP, U&E, albumin, stool culture and C. difficile; IV steroids if confirmed severe (NICE NG130)
Continue mesalazine; avoid loperamide, codeine and NSAIDs; keep drinking
safetyNet: 999: abdominal swelling or severe pain, vomiting, faintness or confusion, chest pain, breathlessness, painful swollen leg
GP calls back within the hour with where to go; follow up after discharge

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Telephone IBD stations test whether you can triage objectively and resist a reasonable-sounding request. Candidates fail by prescribing on a vague history, or by ordering a reluctant patient to hospital without addressing why she doesn’t want to go.

items.fail: Phoning in oral prednisolone after hearing “flare”.
items.why: Ten bloody stools a day with systemic symptoms is acute severe colitis; oral steroids at home are unsafe and delay IV treatment.
items.fix: Score first: stools per day, blood, nocturnal stools, fever, pulse symptoms. If severe, same-day hospital.

items.fail: Not asking about nocturnal stools, fever or dizziness.
items.why: These separate mild from severe. Without them you can’t triage, and examiners mark the gap.
items.fix: Ask for numbers and systemic symptoms explicitly; remember her pulse and temperature can’t be observed by phone.

items.fail: Suggesting loperamide or codeine for the frequency.
items.why: Antimotility drugs and opioids can precipitate toxic dilatation in severe colitis.
items.fix: Advise avoiding loperamide, codeine and NSAIDs; hospital will manage symptoms.

items.fail: Discussing cancer surveillance or a suspected cancer pathway referral today.
items.why: It isn’t relevant to the emergency and uses up time. NICE suspected-cancer guidance has no role here.
items.fix: Mention surveillance briefly for later follow-up (NICE CG118), after the disposition is agreed.

items.fail: “You need to go to A&E” — and nothing about her fears or childcare.
items.why: Ignoring the barrier risks non-attendance and costs Relating to Others marks.
items.fix: Explore the previous admission and surgery fear; reframe; solve childcare and transport together.

items.fail: Ending with “go to hospital” and no call-back or safety-net.
items.why: Remote triage must close the loop. Non-specific advice is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Ring gastroenterology, call her back within a set time, name the 999 symptoms, and use teach-back.
